No. 

The story relies almost entirely on exteriority—focusing heavily on physical actions (operating the ferry, checking the rope, writing in the logbook), sensory descriptions of the cold and fog, and laconic, surface-level dialogue. There is very little interiority; we are given almost no direct access to Ilse's deeper thoughts, feelings, or memories. Even at the end, when a moment of potential emotional conflict arises (the phone call from "Jonas"), it is handled strictly through exterior action (she looks at the screen and puts the phone face down) without any introspection. Because the narrative remains so stoic and external, it does not portray a broad spectrum of emotions or achieve a balance between action and introspection.
